# Audio direction

Decided 2026-10-01, with the first sound set. This doc is to sound what `art-direction.md` is
to colour. Read it before adding, retuning or wiring any sound.

**In one line:** every sound and every piece of music is generated by code in `tools/audio/`, never
recorded or hand-edited. A move's sound is read off its data, not chosen move by move. How loud
a sound is depends on how often it plays, not on how important it feels.

## Why it is generated

This machine has Python 2.7 and nothing else: no numpy, no audio encoder, and no way to record.
WizardSurvivors hit the same wall and built a small synthesiser out of oscillators, filters and
envelopes. `tools/audio/synth.py` is a copy of it. Generating also suits this game: the drawings
are the only hand-made thing in it, and everything around them is built in code.

The limit is real: this pipeline makes cartoon effects and simple synth music, never voices or
recordings. If the kids ever record sounds for their own fighters, those are a separate kind of
file. Nothing here should try to imitate them.

## The sound of the game

The game looks like a kid's drawing come to life, so it sounds like a cartoon, not a gritty
fighter:

- **Swings** are whooshes: filtered noise that swells and fades. A swing gets heavier as the move's
  damage goes up. A sword adds a bright "shing".
- **Hits** are a falling thump under a short bright slap, like paper. The size of the hit goes
  with **knockback** (`SfxCatalog.ForHit`), so the same move sounds bigger at 120% than at 0%.
  That matches the rumble and the camera shake, which already work that way. A hit at kill range
  also gets a crack and a ringing tail. A blocked hit sounds muffled, like hitting cardboard;
  a shield worn through shatters (`shield_break`: a crack, a spray of tinkling shards, and a low
  wobble as he reels).
  A fighter whose weapon is a blade (`FighterData.SlicesOnHit`: EdgeLord) cuts instead of thuds,
  every hit he lands: `hit_slice`, a fast bright zing of steel with a soft thud under it, and
  `hit_slice_heavy` for a big one (Eric, 2026-10-11).
- **Everything tonal is in A major**: the countdown ticks are A, FIGHT! is an A major chord, the
  win fanfare climbs A–C♯–E–A, and the music is in A. The countdown then resolves into the
  music it starts. The one piece in A **minor** is DoomBot's theme - the villain's key - and it
  opens on bare fifths (A and E, no third) so FIGHT! still lands on it cleanly. A story sound
  with a pitch is in A too: the smoke alarm beeps on A7, and the fridge hum and the steam
  whistle sound only A and E, a bare fifth, which fits either key.
- **Talking in a story** is `voice`, a soft rounded blip on A, played every few letters as a
  line types out - one sound for everyone, pitched per fighter at play time
  (`FighterData.VoicePitch`: DoomBot 0.6, Triguy 1.45). It is a blip, never a voice: nothing here
  imitates speech. DoomBot's slammed words use `clang` instead, one per word.

## How a move gets its sound

`SfxCatalog.ForMove` reads the move's data. It returns a sound and the move frame it plays on:

| The move | Sound | When |
|---|---|---|
| a normal holding a sword (`PropArt`/`HeldArt`/`SwingArt` naming one) | `swing_blade` | 4 frames before the hitbox |
| a smash, or 13+ damage | `swing_heavy` | the frame after the charge is released |
| 8+ damage | `swing_medium` | 4 frames before the hitbox |
| anything lighter | `swing_light` | 4 frames before the hitbox |
| a held smash | `smash_charge` looping, rising in pitch | the whole time it is held |
| beam / fireball / volley / single shot | `special_beam` / `_fire` / `_volley` / `_shot` | beam at the start; the rest as the shot leaves |
| a blink (Blur Slash) | `special_glint`, then `special_blink` | the glint lasts 22 frames and peaks on the frame he goes |
| dash, rise, wings, hook, trap, drop, resize, quake, build, bomb | one `special_*` sound each, plus `bomb_fuse` | as the move starts, or as its effect appears |
| a hit drawn as electricity (`ActiveFx.Electric`) | `zap` | when the hit goes live - nothing is swung, so no whoosh leads in |
| a missile (`FxMissile`) / rocket boots (`ActiveFx.Jets`) | `missile` / `jets` | as it leaves / as the flames light |
| a command grab | `special_hook` | as the arms shoot out; the kick that follows is a swing like any other |
| a charged dash (the fireball roll) / a fire cloud | `special_fire` | on release, when the roll goes / as the cloud forms; the rain makes no sound of its own, it would be a drumroll |
| a vent | `steam` or `furnace_blast` | played by the vent itself, because which one depends on his heat |
| a puddle (Triguy's crying) / a bouncing recovery (his trampoline) | `splash` / `boing` | as the puddle hits the floor / on the frame it throws him |
| a walker (the MiniBot) | `special_build` as he sets it down; `minibot_pop` when it goes off | the pop is played by the walker, since it goes off long after the move |

Some sounds belong to a fighter's state, not a move, and are played where that state changes:
`overheat` when a fighter with heat stalls, `burn` on every tick of a burn (quiet, at -20 dBFS,
because it repeats), `creak` when rusty joints seize after a miss, and `clang` when a small hit
bounces off armour (Lug's hard hat), over the muffled blocked-hit thud. EdgeLord's air dash is a
quiet `special_dash`.

Items play their sounds where the item does something, not through `ForMove` - an item's own
swing is a move like any other and gets its whoosh from the rules. Their own: `item_pickup`
(picking one up, a pencil case opening), `item_spray`, `item_snip`, `item_heal` (White-Out),
`item_gust` (the airbrush) and `item_crumple` (the paper ball bouncing). The rest borrow:
`splash` for paint and water, `boing` for the pop-up book, `stomp` for the rubber stamp,
`explosion` for the glitter bomb, `creak` for the thumbtacks, `special_volley` for the crayons,
`special_shot` for the paint tube, `special_build` for the marker's platform, `clang` for the
tinfoil shield sending something back or taking a hit, and the resize, blink and glint sounds for the boosts.

Story scenes play theirs from a script's `sound` line (`.ai/story-mode.md`): `magnet_clink` (a
magnet snapping onto the fridge - short, so three can go up a quarter second apart),
`fridge_hum` (two seconds of compressor, soft at both ends), `smoke_alarm` (three shrill beeps)
and `steam_whistle` (DoomBot's meltdown: a shriek climbing out of a hiss). A page put up on the
fridge clinks like a magnet; a whip pan borrows `item_gust`.

The whoosh starts 4 frames early on purpose. A whoosh is loudest about a third of the way through,
so starting early puts the rush of air on the hit, not after it.

**Why the sound comes from the data:** five fighters with seventeen moves each is eighty-five
choices. Every rebalance would have to keep them in step, and a new kid's fighter would arrive
silent. Because the sound comes from the data, a new fighter has sound the day it is added. When
the rules get a move wrong, set `MoveData.Sound` on that move; do not add a special case to the
rules.

**Nobody on the project can hear the output.** So `RegressionChecks` prints which sound each
fighter's moves got, one line per fighter. Read it after adding a fighter. It has already caught
"sl**edge**hammer" counting as a blade, and summoned swords going "pew".

## Loudness follows how often a sound plays

Every file is normalised to a peak target set in `REGISTRY` in `tools/audio/sfx.py`, and the game
plays everything at 0 dB. **The registry is the mix.** To change the balance, edit one number
there and rebuild; do not add `VolumeDb` at call sites.

| How often | Peak | Members |
|---|---|---|
| once a match | −3 to −5 dBFS | `ko_blast`, `game_set`, `count_go`, `explosion`, `hit_smash` |
| a few times a stock | −6 to −9 dBFS | `hit_heavy`, `hit_medium`, `count_tick`, `special_quake`, `special_beam`, `special_blink`, `shield_break` |
| every exchange | −10 to −14 dBFS | swings, most specials, `hit_light`, `hit_block`, menu select |
| constantly | −15 dBFS and below | `bomb_fuse`, `smash_charge` (−17), `ui_move` (−21) |

A sound with no transient - the fridge hum, the smoke alarm, the steam whistle - is set by its
A-weighted loudness instead, since its peak says little: the whistle as loud as `game_set`, the
alarm as `count_go`, the hum (all low end) about as loud as a talking blip.

Music sits under all of it at −9 dB (`MusicPlayer.VolumeDb`). Every track peaks at −3 dBFS, so
that one number is the whole balance between music and effects. While the game is paused the
music drops a further 12 dB.

## Music

`tools/audio/music.py` writes the menu loop, a battle loop for every stage, the story and DoomBot
loops and a victory sting, mono, at 22050 Hz - each loop 26 to 44 seconds and 1.1 to 1.9 MB, in a
repo with no LFS.

Most of it is cartoon music. That was Eric's call on 2026-10-04 ("something more fun"). On
2026-10-18 the battle music went action ("more like actiony battle"), the menu went chill ("less
like annoying whistling music"), and every stage got its own battle loop, fitting the place
(`StageData.Music`; a story's boss still fights to DoomBot's theme). The harmony of the cartoon
pieces leans on secondary dominants (C♯7, F♯7, B7, E7): a chord that wants to fall to the next one
is most of what makes music sound like a cartoon.

- **menu** — 88 BPM, lightly swung lo-fi. An electric piano laying down rootless seventh chords,
  a vibraphone with the tune and room around it, an upright bass on one and the and of two, and a
  soft felt kick, a snap and a shaker. Amaj7–F♯m7–Bm7–E9 twice (the second time through Dmaj7), then
  the bridge Dmaj7–C♯m7–Bm7–E9, whose E9 pulls into the top. It plays unbroken from the title
  through fighter and stage select, because `MusicPlayer` lives on `GameRoot` and not on any one
  screen, so nothing in it is bright or busy - and nothing whistles.
- **battle** (Fridge Door, and any stage without its own) — 152 BPM action rock in A: a four-bar
  riff of power chords chugging eighths (accents 3-3-2), the hero's theme on a driven two-saw lead
  over A–F–G–A, the theme soaring over D–F–G–A with the drums four on the floor and brass stabbing
  under it, and a half-time build on E climbing F–G under a snare roll into the top. Power chords
  have no third, so FIGHT!'s A major chord lands on them and the tune can lean minor.
- **battle_plains** (Open Plains) — 138 BPM, A major, an adventure: a steel-string strum
  galloping (an eighth and two sixteenths a beat), a march on the drums, the tune on brass.
- **battle_rooftops** (City Rooftops) — 120 BPM, A minor, night-time synthwave: a synth arpeggio
  running sixteenths round Am–F–C–G like lights going by, a pulsing octave bass, a long lead.
- **battle_bigshow** (Big Show) — 184 BPM, A major, punk rock: open power chords thrashed in
  eighths, the bass doubling them, kick and snare flat out, a shout-along tune. Its speakers thump
  on the beat (`SpeakerBlast`, 20 frames a beat, near enough 184 BPM).
- **battle_playground** (Playground) — the bouncy ska romp that was the only battle music before:
  164 BPM, offbeat chops, an octave-bouncing bass, a handheld-console lead called and answered by
  cartoon brass, and a slide whistle back to the top. A game, for where the fighting is one.
- **battle_site** (Building Site) — 126 BPM, A minor, industrial: the machines are the band - a
  kick on every beat, a hammer on an anvil for the backbeat, pistons ticking sixteenths, a muted
  power chord grinding, a robot's bleeps, steam venting at the end of every phrase, and a low
  conveyor-belt riff.
- **battle_kitchen** (Kitchen Counter) — 108 BPM funk on A7 and D7: a clav-like chop on the
  sixteenths, a popping bass, the horns with the tune, and pots and pans in the drums - a saucepan
  for the cowbell, a spoon on a woodblock for the clave.
- **story** — 100 BPM, lightly swung, sixteen bars, under the talking in story scenes. A storybook
  tiptoe: a plucked oom-pah (pizzicato bass on one and three, violins on two and four), the tune
  on a glockenspiel, a bassoon telling the jokes, a triangle at the top of each half. It opens on
  A–A♯dim7–Bm7–E7, the chord that sneaks; then A7 leaning into D, and D turning to D minor for a
  wink. The bridge gives the bassoon D♯dim7 to creep up and F♯7 to tumble down, and ends on E7.
  It has to stay out of the way of talking, so it has no drums and nothing sustained, and the
  glock never plays below 830 Hz, above the talking blips (under 760 Hz). In 250–800 Hz it
  carries 5 dB less than the menu, though overall, A-weighted, it is nearly as loud.
- **doombot** — DoomBot's boss theme, 140 BPM, twenty-four bars, in A minor. First a villain's
  march: a tuba and a kick on every beat, an anvil for the backbeat, growling trombones going
  DUN, DUN, DUN, da-DUNN while the bass sinks a half step a bar under an organ chord, then
  F–B♭–E and a stop - "dun, dun, DUNNN" - and the machine lets off steam. Then the factory floor:
  a palm-muted power chord chugging every eighth (accents 3-3-2), the organ stamping one figure
  down Am–G–F–E, a robot's bleeps under it. Then the overheat, power chords climbing A–B♭–B–C
  under an organ siren and a snare roll, and the march home on F–Dm–E into the stop again. On
  his last stock the game plays it 1.25 times as fast, pitch and all (`MusicPlayer.SetSpeed`):
  nothing in it is faster than sixteenths, and those only on quiet parts, so it stays clear at 175.
- **victory** — a three-second sting for a story fight won, played once (`MusicPlayer.PlayOnce`),
  150 BPM. A trumpet runs up A–C♯–E in a triplet and tops out, then the cartoon cadence F–G–A
  (♭VI–♭VII–I), a brass "bah" on each, the last held with a timpani, a cymbal, a snare roll
  into it, and the story's glockenspiel running up two octaves of A.

Nobody on the project can hear them, so the parts are written to rules that can be checked on
paper: chord tones on the strong beats, passing notes only on the weak ones, and no semitone rub
between a tune and the chord under it. Each track's balance is one table in `music.py`
(`MENU_MIX`, `BATTLE_MIX`, one per stage like `BIG_MIX` and `SITE_MIX`, `STORY_MIX`, `DOOM_MIX`, `VICTORY_MIX`), like the registry is for
effects. It was set by measuring each part, A-weighted, against the whole while that part plays.

The loops loop with no gap or click. Notes and reverb that ring past the end are wrapped round
onto the start, so nothing gets cut off at the loop point, and so is the filter that halves the sample
rate: started cold, it put a one-sample tick at the seam of any loop that ends loud. A `smpl`
chunk marks each file as a loop, and Godot's importer reads it (`edit/loop_mode=0`, Detect From
WAV). `SfxPlayer.Load` also sets the loop in code, in case an import setting ever overrides the
chunk. `RegressionChecks` warns if any of the four loops imported without it. The victory sting
is written without the chunk, so it plays once and stops - and `RegressionChecks` fails if it
ever loops.

## Godot side

- **`SfxPlayer`** and **`MusicPlayer`** are children of `GameRoot`. Like everything else in this
  project, they are built in code, and they create the `Music` and `SFX` buses at runtime. There
  is a hard limiter at −1 dBFS on `SFX`.
- Every sound is loaded once at boot and played from a fixed set of players (16 that pan with the
  fight, 6 for menus). A repeat of the same sound within 35 ms is dropped, so a volley does not
  stack into one blast.
- Fight sounds pan with where they happen, at half strength: both players sit in front of the same
  TV, so a hit should never vanish into one speaker. Pitch varies by ±5% on each play, so the
  same hit twice does not sound mechanical.
- The smash charge hum belongs to the fighter, not the shared players. That way it pauses with the
  match and goes when he goes.
- `MusicPlayer.Play` crossfades to a loop. `PlayOnce` plays a sting: whatever was playing fades
  out under it, but the sting starts at full level, because its first note is the point of it,
  and silence follows it. A loop asked for while the sting is still sounding waits for it to
  end: the scene after a story win asks for the story theme on its first line, and would
  otherwise fade the sting out half a second in. `SetSpeed` speeds up whatever is playing,
  pitch and all; changing track puts the speed back to normal.

## Adding a sound

1. Write a builder in `tools/audio/sfx.py` and add it to `REGISTRY` with a peak level from the
   table above. A builder missing from the registry does not ship.
2. Add the name to `SfxCatalog.AllNames`, and to `ForMove` if a kind of move should use it.
3. `python tools/audio/build.py <name>`, then `"$GODOT_BIN" --headless --path . --import`.
4. Boot headless and read the `RegressionChecks: sounds` lines.
5. Commit the builder **and** the generated `.wav`.

## Don't

- Hand-edit anything in `assets/sfx/` or `assets/music/`. Edit the builder and run it again.
- Ship stereo. Godot will not pan a stereo sound, and nothing here needs stereo.
- Put a fade on a loop: on a loop, the fade itself is the click.
- Use the module-level `random` in `tools/audio/`; use only seeded instances, so a rebuild comes
  out byte-identical.
- Pick sounds move by move in C#. Use `MoveData.Sound` for the exceptions.
- Set a sound's loudness by how important it feels. Set it by how often it plays.
